title: Black Myth: Wukong
subtitle: Retracing the Journey to the West · Seeking Destiny Amid Ancient Architecture
description: Black Myth: Wukong is an action role-playing game by Game Science, based on Journey to the West. Over several years, the game team traversed hundreds of ancient temples and monasteries across China, meticulously scanning countless nationally protected cultural heritage sites, infusing every frame with the millennia-old beauty of Chinese craftsmanship. This article follows in the footsteps of the Destined One, retracing the journey westward, seeking true 'destiny' among ancient shrines and stone carvings.

route.title: Black Myth: Wukong — The Destined One's Journey West
route.intro:
Having seen the future, why do you not bow?
On August 20, 2024, a monkey set out from the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit, stirring up the entire gaming world. Within three days, it sold over ten million copies, leaving players around the globe stunned — not only by the exhilarating combat, but by the breathtakingly beautiful ancient architectural scenes in every frame. Few know that during development, Game Science's art team traversed hundreds of ancient temples and grottoes across Shanxi, Chongqing, Fujian, Sichuan, Shandong, Tianjin, Shaanxi, Zhejiang and beyond, performing millimeter-precision 3D scans of countless nationally protected cultural sites. Those time-worn murals, colored sculptures weathered for a thousand years, and interlocking wooden structures were faithfully transported into the digital world. Black Myth: Wukong tells a story set after the pilgrimage. The Victorious Fighting Buddha, unwilling to be bound by the Heavenly Court's rules, resigns his Buddha seat and returns to the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit. The heavens rage, dispatching Erlang Shen with celestial troops to surround the mountain. After a great battle between the Great Sage Equal to Heaven and Erlang Shen, he dissolves into the Six Roots — eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind — scattered across the four directions, seized by various demon kings. Years later, a monkey of unknown origin — the 'Destined One' — sets out from the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit, following the old westward road to defeat each demon king who holds a piece of the Great Sage's power. Every temple he enters, every grotto he passes, every colored sculpture he beholds — all are real thousand-year-old protected sites. Let us join the Destined One on this epic journey spanning the three realms.

stops.title: Prologue: Mountain of Flowers and Fruit — The Great Sage Returns
stops.content:
The story begins on a mountain.

An old monkey sits beneath an ancient tree at the summit, telling a group of young monkeys the same story told a thousand times: the Great Sage Equal to Heaven, Sun Wukong, escorted the Tang Monk west to obtain the scriptures, was crowned the Victorious Fighting Buddha, and ascended to the immortal ranks. But unwilling to be bound by the rules of the Celestial Palace, he shed his robe, dispersed his Buddha light, and returned alone to the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit in Eastern Divine Continent.

How could the Heavenly Court let this stand? The True Lord Erlang, leading the Seven Sages of Plum Mountain and a hundred thousand celestial soldiers, surrounded the mountain.

That battle raged for seven days and seven nights. Seventy-two transformations against the Eight-Nine Arcane Arts, the Compliant Golden-Hooped Rod against the Tri-Pointed Double-Edged Blade. From the Water Curtain Cave to the Southern Heavenly Gate, from the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit to Guanjiang Estuary. Finally, Erlang Shen summoned his Howling Celestial Dog, and the Great Sage swung his staff — mountains crumbled, the earth split, and golden light scattered in all directions.

When the dust settled, the monkey was gone. Only six radiant objects remained on the ground, each flying off in a different direction.

These were the 'Six Roots' — eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind. After the Great Sage's nirvana, the Six Roots scattered across the three realms, picked up by various demon kings who each claimed one, setting themselves up as rulers.

From then on, the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit had no Great Sage.

Only a legend remained — that once every few hundred years, a monkey would emerge from the mountain. People called him the 'Destined One.' He would retrace the westward journey, defeat the demons holding the Great Sage's relics, gather the Six Roots, and bring the Great Sage back.

You are the Destined One of this age.

The mountain mist parts, revealing a winding path leading beyond the mountains. With the Golden-Hooped Rod on your back — though it is really just some random iron staff — you leap into the air. This journey west, awaited by countless people for so many years, has finally begun.

stops.title: Chapter 1: Black Wind Mountain — Traces of a Zen Monastery
stops.content: The Destined One leaves the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit and plunges into the vast, dense Black Wind Mountain. The path grows deeper, the forest thicker. Suddenly, the view opens — a burned-out ancient temple stands starkly in the moonlight. Amid the broken walls and crumbling foundations, wisps of blue smoke curl upward, and blackened beams silently tell the story of a great fire's desolation. This scene inevitably reminds you of the thousand-year-old temple in Quanzhou, Fujian — Kaiyuan Temple. Its twin pagodas pierce the clouds, its mulberry-lotus Dharma-realm has witnessed over thirteen hundred years of rise and fall. The east and west pagodas still stand tall, their Song-dynasty stone structures shimmering warmly in the sunlight, bearing witness to Quanzhou's millennium of prosperity as a world maritime trade center. Was this Zen monastery not once just as glorious? Heading deeper into the mountains, you find that every rock and blade of grass on Black Wind Mountain breathes with stone-carving artistry — because many of its mountain textures were inspired by Sichuan's Anyue Grottoes. In Anyue County, it is said that 'where there is a cliff, there is a Buddha; where there is a mountain, there is a niche.' Over a hundred thousand statues from the Tang to Song dynasties are scattered through the countryside, less grand than the famous great grottoes but possessing an intimate zen-like connection with nature. Wandering through them is like walking through a history of Buddhist art spread across the open fields. The Zen monastery ruins on Black Wind Mountain always evoke those humble yet timeless ancient buildings hidden deep in the mountains — Zhejiang Jingning's Shisi Temple, hidden deep in the She ethnic township's mountains, its gate, main hall, and sutra pillars preserving Yuan-dynasty structures, the whole temple blending seamlessly with ancient willows and deep forests. That isolated tranquility was the very character of this abandoned monastery. In southern Sichuan, Nanchong's Lifeng Temple preserves a complete Yuan-dynasty wooden structure, a precious example of southern Yuan architecture; and Mianyang's Pingyang Fujun Que, this pair of Eastern Han stone watchtowers are supreme examples of existing Han watchtowers, with over five dozen niches of Buddhist sculptures added during the Southern Dynasties five hundred years later — one structure spanning two eras, a superposition that is the most wonderful aspect of history itself, just as beneath the ashes of Black Wind Mountain's ruins lie the greed and obsession of Elder Jinchi. Deep in Black Wind Mountain stood Guanyin Zen Monastery, once a thriving great temple. The aged abbot, Elder Jinchi, who had lived for two hundred and seventy years, was consumed by greed and sought to steal the Tang Monk's brocade kasaya. He sent his disciple Guangzhi to set a night fire — but the blaze spiraled out of control, and the entire monastery was reduced to ashes. His entire collection of kasayas, accumulated over two centuries, burned along with the monastery. Only a twisted bronze bell remained, still hanging there, humming with the wind. As you draw near, the bronze bell suddenly shakes violently — a monk cloaked in golden light, wielding a double-headed monk's spade, emerges from the flames. Not Jinchi, but his senior disciple Guangzhi, a martial monk who trained to the point of madness, his soul still guarding these ruins after death. He swings his staff, the shadow of his strikes dense as a rainstorm. After great effort you subdue him, and just before he disperses, Guangzhi mutters, 'Master... the kasaya...' One died for greed, the other trapped by obsession. Pressing deeper into the forest, you arrive at a tranquil valley. By the stream, a massive black bear spirit sits in meditation. Behind Elder Jinchi's ambition was always this Black Wind King — after that great fire, he fled, and now, having somehow obtained the Great Sage's 'Eye Root,' his power grows by the day. He regards you with a mix of disdain and curiosity: 'Another monkey? Hah, that Sun Wukong was nothing special.' This black bear spirit is the same one from Journey to the West, later taken by Guanyin to be the guardian mountain god of Mount Putuo. You fight him from outside the cave to within, then from the cave to the mountain peak. With your final blow, his body splits open, and a radiant, eye-like object flies forth — the Great Sage's Eye Root. Your vision suddenly expands, revealing the finest details of heaven and earth — dewdrops hidden behind pine needles, the patterns of every pebble beneath the stream. This 'Fiery Golden Eyes' not only pierces disguises but also discerns demonic trickery. The journey to Black Wind Mountain grants you the first of the Great Sage's relics, and shows you how greed and obsession can transform a Buddhist sanctuary into a ghostly realm. Looking back, the ash-covered monastery still stands in the twilight — a reminder of how many ancient temples throughout history have been destroyed by war, consumed by greed, and rebuilt time and again over the ruins. It is an almost eternal tension: destruction and rebirth, greed and cultivation, fire and zen.
stops.poem:
Within Black Wind Mountain, an old Zen hall, a night of greed brought calamity for all.
Jinchi dreams of kasayas in death's embrace, the bear's first taste of fiery-eyed grace.

stops.title: Chapter 2: Yellow Wind Ridge — The Calamity of the Wind-Fixing Pearl
stops.content: After obtaining the Eye Root, the Destined One continues westward. Gradually, the mountains turn yellow, the trees thin, and a bitter, sandy taste rises in the air. This is Yellow Wind Ridge — a sky-darkening haze of yellow sand, the wind laced with gravel that stings the face. This was once a vital route from the Western Regions to the Central Plains, teeming with merchant caravans and camel trains. But since the demon lord Yellow Wind Great Sage took over, raising endless sandstorms that scour the land for a hundred miles, nothing grows here. His wind is so fierce it can scatter souls and shatter bones. It is said this gale has raged for a century, toppling walls, burying fields, so that even wild rats dare not burrow here. Walking through the sandstorm, you glimpse the silhouettes of stone mountains in the distance — wind-eroded rock faces densely covered in Buddha statues. This is no illusion; it is the weathered stone of Yungang Grottoes. In the 5th century, Northern Wei craftsmen carved forty-five caves and over fifty thousand Buddha statues into the southern face of Wuzhou Mountain, stretching for a kilometer. Fifteen centuries of wind and sand have blurred the outlines of some statues, yet the compassion in their eyes and brows still pierces through time. The fragmentary Buddhas faintly visible on Yellow Wind Ridge's bare rock faces are the game artists' recreation of Yungang's weathered textures — these stone Buddhas reshaped by natural forces possess a weathered grandeur far beyond their original freshness. Beyond this grotto zone stands an ancient pagoda — Shanxi Lingqiu's Jueshan Temple Pagoda, its octagonal dense-eave brick tower exuding calm amid the swirling yellow sand. This Liao-dynasty brick pagoda has withstood earthquakes, its layers adorned with exquisite brick-carved bracket sets, a model of northern Liao pagoda architecture. The sand strikes the tower body with a rustling sound, like chanting from a thousand years ago. Further off, Shuozhou's Chongfu Temple Amitabha Hall retains its Jin-dynasty colored sculptures and brilliant glazed tiles, its window lattices carved in over a dozen styles, none identical — even in the most violent sandstorms, someone was painstakingly crafting beauty. Through the broken walls, a stone bridge spans a dry riverbed. At the bridgehead stands a Tiger Vanguard — tiger-headed, human-bodied, gripping a nine-ring broadsword, motionless in the storm. 'To cross this bridge, you must first pass me,' he growls, his voice like grinding gravel. The Tiger Vanguard is Yellow Wind Great Sage's deadliest enforcer. His blade style is sweeping and brutal, each stroke carving deep gorges into the sand. You dodge and weave around him, your staff flying — finally, on the thirtieth exchange, you strike his sword back, shattering his grip. The nine-ring blade clatters to the ground. With a grunt, he dissolves into a pile of sand. Later you learn that the Tiger Vanguard was once a hero of the mountain, forced into service. His fighting spirit had never truly left — this battle was his true release. Defeating the Tiger Vanguard, you reach the lair of the Yellow Wind Great Sage — an ancient city ruin half-buried by dunes. The Yellow Wind Great Sage sits at the eye of the storm, swirling yellow sand around him like a sand dragon. 'Another monkey? Even Sun Wukong lost his way in my winds back then — and you, a little whelp, dare approach?' He speaks the truth. In Journey to the West, the Yellow Wind Monster indeed blinded the Great Sage Sun with his samadhi wind. Now he has obtained the Great Sage's 'Ear Root' — the wind, footsteps, heartbeats — nothing can hide from his hearing. This battle is fought in the wind — you cannot see him, but he hears every breath you take. You close your eyes, ignoring the storm, listening with your heart. Amid the howling sand, you finally catch a faint sound — the 'Ear Root' pulsing within the wind column. Gathering your strength, your staff strikes straight into the wind's eye. The Yellow Wind Great Sage lets out a piercing shriek, his body deflating like a torn bag. An ear-shaped spiritual object falls into your palm — the Ear Root. In an instant, all sounds cease. You hear the crisp fall of individual sand grains, a rainstorm three thousand miles away, and the ancient riverbed beneath your feet — where fish once leaped and water once splashed. Pocketing the Ear Root, the sandstorm stops. A corner of blue sky, unseen for a century, peeks through the yellow clouds. You shoulder your pack and continue westward — ahead, even greater demon kings await.
stops.poem:
A hundred fathoms of yellow sand lay waste, the tiger falls at the bridge in haste.
The ear root stills, hearing through the air, the storm subsides, revealing blue laid bare.

stops.title: Chapter 3: Little Western Paradise — The Suspended Sculptures of the Heavens
stops.content: Crossing the ruins of Yellow Wind Ridge, the sound of wind and sand fades. Ahead, the mountains grow higher, capped with snow, veiled in mist at the waist. A small path descends from the mountain, marked by a stele at its entrance — 'Little Western Paradise.' The moment you push through the gate, you are utterly overwhelmed by what you see. Heaven filled with Buddhas. Not a metaphor — literally. From the walls to the ceiling, every inch of the hall is packed with dense sculptures: bodhisattvas seated in lotus position on clouds, celestial maidens with robes flowing between beams, flying apsaras circling upward around the bracket sets, thousands of Buddhas layered all the way to the dome. Gold, vermilion, azurite, emerald green — a riot of color unlike anything in the mortal world. This is 'suspended sculpture.' Using techniques of suspended shaping in a confined space, the artists made the Western Pure Land 'grow' out of the walls. This scene in the game is almost a perfect replica of the real-world Thousand-Buddha Nunnery in Xixian County, Shanxi — also known as 'Little Western Paradise.' In the Ming dynasty's Chongzhen era, Zen Master Dongming built this small nunnery atop Phoenix Mountain. Inside the Mahavira Hall, artisans used suspended sculpture techniques to stack an entire dazzling Western Pure Land. In just one hundred and ninety square meters, there are over a thousand statues — the largest over three meters tall, the smallest the size of a thumb — yet none are repeated, and none are anything less than exquisite. It is a suffocating splendor — standing in the center of the hall, looking up, you feel as small as a speck of dust, while the Buddha's land is right before you. But the 'Little Western Paradise' in the game, though outwardly resplendent, is a trap set by the Yellow Brow King. The Yellow Brow King — the Yellow Brow Boy, disciple of Maitreya Buddha, descended to the mortal realm as a demon — has built a 'New Great Thunderclap Monastery' here. To everyone who enters, he says: 'Having seen the future, why do you not bow?' He preaches and spreads the dharma in Maitreya's name, deceiving all. His evil arts shroud the entire 'Little Western Paradise' in an unnatural cold light — the suspended sculptures are beautiful, but with an inhuman beauty; the Buddhas have kind brows and kind eyes, yet the corners of their smiles hide a sinister chill. The atmosphere of this Buddha-land illusion pervades every inch of Little Western Paradise — while in the real world, similar Zen spirit can be found scattered across many more places. In Changqing, Shandong, Lingyan Temple nestles among encircling mountains; its Thousand-Buddha Hall houses forty Song-dynasty colored clay arhats, each one vividly distinct, which Liang Qichao once praised as 'the finest sculptures under heaven.' At Liubu Town at the foot of Mount Tai, Shentong Temple's Four-Gate Pagoda has stood quietly for a full fourteen hundred years. This is China's oldest surviving single-story pavilion-style stone pagoda, built in the seventh year of the Sui dynasty's Daye era, with a square body and a gate on each side. Its form is almost simple to the point of plainness, yet it possesses a power beyond time. Outside Ping顺's Hongni Village, Minghui Master Pagoda stands quietly on the riverbank — a Five Dynasties stone pagoda, exquisitely carved and gracefully shaped, standing tall through centuries. At Fufeng, Baoji, Shaanxi, Famen Temple Site holds a Tang-dynasty underground palace beneath its grounds, the radiance of the Buddha's finger relic undimmed for a thousand years — this compassion and faith toward the future is the true meaning of the 'future' that Yellow Brow speaks of. To pass through Little Western Paradise, you must first overcome two trials. 'Bubai' is a monk as white as snow, wielding an ice sword. His swordplay is extremely fierce — each strike unleashes bone-piercing arctic energy, freezing the ground, freezing waterfalls, freezing your movements. You must contend with him on the slippery ice, sliding away from his ice blade, smashing your staff into the ice to send up showers of frozen shards. When he falls, his body shatters into a pool of ice crystals. Even more troublesome than 'Bubai' is 'Bukong' — an old monk with a staff who can manipulate space with Sanskrit chanting. Each of his Buddha's names creates transparent sutra-character walls in the air, trapping people within. You dash left and right in the prison of sutras, and finally find a flaw in that rapidly spinning sutra wall — the character 'Empty' is missing one stroke. Complete it with a blow of your staff, and the sutra wall shatters with a sound. As Bukong dies, he slumps to the ground, murmuring: 'All beings suffer... Not empty, yet not empty.' His obsession was to save all beings — but he walked the demonic path while wearing the monk's robe, deceiving himself and others. When you finally defeat the Yellow Brow King, he falls to the ground, a wry smile on his face: 'You think you have won? Everything here — every Buddha, every piece of gold leaf — is false. Maitreya never came. The future never came. You and I are nothing but specks of dust in this Buddha-land dream.' He dissolves. In that moment, the suspended Buddha-land loses all color — gold leaf peels away, paint fades, and the myriad Buddhas and celestial beings revert to piles of clay. In the real-world Xixian, the suspended sculptures of the Thousand-Buddha Nunnery are the opposite — four hundred years on, they remain as brilliant as ever, proving that 'when the Buddha is in the heart, there is no illusion.' The Great Sage's 'Nose Root' falls from the Yellow Brow King. Your nose clears — you suddenly smell sandalwood, ink, the fresh scent of rain-soaked earth, the one real thing in this false Buddha-land: the true fragra... (line truncated to 2000 chars)
stops.poem:
Golden suspended forms mask a cunning scheme, chanting shatters the wall, asking of empty dream.
Yellow Brow speaks falsely of a Western heavenly bower — the Buddha lives in the heart, not in the tower.

stops.title: Chapter 4: Spidersilk Ridge · Yellow Flower Abbey — Bonds of Passion Hard to Sever
stops.content: With the Nose Root, the Destined One leaves Little Western Paradise and enters a sweltering, misty mountain range. The air suddenly turns sticky — not from heat, but from countless ultra-fine threads floating in the air, tickling the skin, clogging the nostrils. Between the trees ahead, enormous spiderwebs hang between ancient trees, shimmering with an eerie silver light in the sun. This is Spidersilk Ridge. And at the mountain entrance, clinging to a sheer cliff, hangs a complex of buildings reminiscent of Hanging Temple — halls of Confucianism, Buddhism, and Daoism connected by plank paths, embedded vertically in the cliff face. An old poem says, 'Hanging Temple, half a sky high, three马尾 hanging in the air.' This architectural marvel suspended on a precipice mirrors the web-like layered spatial structure of the Spider Cave. Those halls that seem ready to fall at any moment have actually stood for fifteen hundred years on the mechanical principle of chiseling holes and inserting beams — just as the Destined One must find that unbreakable thread of survival among the strands of silk. This is a two-layered world: above, the overlapping spiderweb caverns; below, a strange Daoist temple called 'Yellow Flower Abbey.' Dwelling in the Spider Cave is Violet Spider — mistress of the cavern, queen of the spider spirits. She has an old grudge against Sun Wukong: in Journey to the West, Wukong beat her seven junior sisters and stirred up her bath pool. Now, with the Great Sage's 'Tongue Root,' Violet Spider's power has grown immensely, and her silk wraps the entire mountain in layers. Beneath her are a group of beguiling yet lethal spider sisters — each beautiful, but with fine, venomous fangs revealed when they smile. You cut through strands and break webs, groping forward through the immense Spider Cave. The cave is a labyrinth — cave within cave, silk behind silk. Some threads glue you in place; others disguised as ordinary rock give way at a touch. You once lost your way for a long time in a deep tunnel, finding your way out only by following the reflections on the threads — in that moment, you deeply felt the terror of the Tang Monk when he was bound here. The spider sisters attack in turn — some spit paralyzing venom threads, some teleport between webs for ambushes, others transform into giant venomous spiders, their eight long legs like eight spears. Each battle requires finding gaps among the threads, slipping through the webbing. After defeating the six sisters, the eldest, Violet Spider, awaits you at the deepest point. She is a true fusion of beauty and poison. Above the waist, a stunningly beautiful woman; below, a massive, glossy black spider abdomen. Her voice is as sweet as a song: 'Little monkey, you are too late — the Great Sage's tongue has tasted the finest nectar from the heavenly banquet. Now that it has reached my mouth, I must savor every flavor of this mortal world.' With a flick of her long tongue, every strand of silk in the cave tightens at once. The silk strangles the breath from you; darkness closes in. But at the critical moment, you remember the Great Sage's Tongue Root — not for eating, not for tasting — but for savoring every flavor of the world. You put away your staff, open your mouth, and bite through the silk wrapped around your throat. It tastes like rust, like mugwort, like tears — and following that taste, you find the densest cluster of silk, and drive your staff straight to its heart. Violet Spider's shrill scream echoes through the cave. She disperses — along with all the cave's silk, which turns to powder. The Tongue Root falls into your palm, and a strange sensation spreads from your tongue through your entire body: you taste the earth's must, the nectar's sweetness, the rust's bitterness, the sweat's saltiness — every flavor of the human world, all in a single thought. Leaving the Spider Cave and crossing a ridge, you come to Yellow Flower Abbey — home to the Hundred-Eyed Demon Lord, Violet Spider's senior brother. His thousand-eye golden light wounds invisibly, and the entire abbey is shrouded in poison mist. The design of Yellow Flower Abbey draws deep inspiration from several treasures of Shanxi: Guanyin Hall, where Confucian, Buddhist, and Daoist figures gather in a small hall, the Ming-dynasty suspended heavens stacked with gods; the oppressive sense of the Hundred-Eyed Demon Lord's thousand eyes opening simultaneously draws from this visual density. Zezhou's Jade Emperor Temple in Jincheng, where the Yuan-dynasty master sculptor Liu Yuan created the Twenty-Eight Mansions colored sculptures, each riding a mythical beast in a different pose, as if the stars themselves had taken human form — this concept of 'making the celestial visible' gives the Hundred-Eyed Demon Lord his hundred divine personas' visual impact. Gaoping's Gaoping Iron Buddha Temple in Jincheng, where the Twenty-Four Devas colored sculptures feature exaggerated limbs and fierce expressions, known as the 'crown of Ming sculpture.' Traditional Buddhist statues emphasize serene compassion, but the Iron Buddha Temple's deva statues are full of dynamism and power, as if about to leap off their altars. The design language of the monstrous Daoists in Yellow Flower Abbey originates here — exaggerated limbs, dramatic expressions, and a breakthrough in traditional representation. And in the deep mountains of Lingchuan, Jincheng, Xixi Erxian Temple's Jin-dynasty main hall is flanked by two dressing towers on east and west — a unique pavilion form dedicated to goddesses found nowhere else in the country, imbued with the unique religious character of the Shangdang region. It was also in the guise of 'daughters' that Violet Spider and her sisters ruled Spidersilk Ridge... (line truncated to 2000 chars)
stops.poem:
Ten thousand strands of silk bind the lonely peak, six sisters wail with venom's reek.
The tongue tastes every bitter flavor of mortal toil — beyond Guanyin Hall, the story is still uncoiled.

stops.title: Chapter 5: Flaming Mountain · Plantain Cave — The Karmic Fire of the Red Lotus
stops.content: Leaving Spidersilk Ridge and continuing westward, the air grows hotter and drier. On the distant horizon, a dark red ribbon trembles in the distorted heat haze. Flaming Mountain. This is where the Great Sage once kicked over Taishang Laojun's Eight Trigrams Furnace, and a single furnace brick fell to earth. Eight hundred miles of flames burn unceasingly; even a body of bronze and iron could not endure the heat. Back then, the Tang Monk and his disciples could only pass this way thanks to the Plantain Fan of Princess Iron Fan. Now, this place is ruled by the Bull Demon King — Sun Wukong's sworn elder brother, once the Great Sage Who Flattens Heaven. The Bull Demon King has obtained the Great Sage's 'Body Root' — the very power of the Compliant Golden-Hooped Rod itself. Unlike the demon lords before him: he is both demon and man, both fiend and father. He is not a pure villain, but a tough man ground down by fate: his wife Princess Iron Fan sits alone in her empty chamber, his son Red Boy was taken by Guanyin as Sudhana, his brother Wukong 'betrayed' him by becoming a Buddha first. He occupies this Flaming Mountain not merely for power — he is waiting, waiting for the day Red Boy returns, waiting for the day his once-legendary brother comes to share a drink with him. But Princess Iron Fan refuses to see him. She has locked herself in the Plantain Cave, sealing the entrance with her fan. She hates her husband, hates him for driving Red Boy to Guanyin, and hates him for his powerlessness. The stones at the cave mouth are hot enough to fry an egg, but Princess Iron Fan lives inside — perhaps her heart burns even hotter. As you approach the foot of Flaming Mountain, the first to block your path is not the Bull Demon King, but Red Boy. No — he is no longer the three-year-old child in a red bellyband. He is now a young man wreathed in flames, exuding murderous intent. He escaped from Guanyin Bodhisattva's Purple Bamboo Forest — centuries of cultivation by the Bodhisattva's side did not temper his ferocity; instead, it refined his samadhi true fire to a level that could incinerate heaven and earth. 'My father does not listen to me. My mother cannot control me. Even Guanyin Bodhisattva cannot stop me. And you — a nameless monkey — who do you think you are to come here?' Without another word, Red Boy raises his hands, and twin fire dragons surge straight at you. This is the most unforgettable hard-fought battle of the entire journey west. Red Boy moves like crimson lightning, each charge sending up walls of flame dozens of meters high. You leap and weave between fire and lava, your golden staff glowing red-hot in the inferno. In the heat of battle, Red Boy suddenly stops in midair, crosses his arms, and chants — every flame on the entire mountain seems drawn to his palms. Then he thrusts both hands forward, and a fireball ten spans in diameter hurtles toward you. You raise your golden staff to withstand it — the staff can grow and shrink, lengthen and shorten. With a thought, the iron rod spreads horizontally like an iron wall before you. The fireball crashes against the staff, exploding into a rain of sparks, like a downpour of fire. At last, Red Boy falls to the ground, exhausted, gasping for air. He does not cry, nor beg for mercy — just stares coldly at you and says: 'I wanted to be a hero too. But heroes... are titles others bestow.' He dissolves into a wisp of blue smoke, either returning to the Purple Bamboo Forest or vanishing to some other place. Having defeated the son, the father finally shows himself. The Bull Demon King strides slowly from the mouth of Flaming Mountain, each step shaking the earth. His form is even more enormous than any legend described — not a bull demon, but a walking mountain. 'Red Boy lost?' His voice is low as tectonic movement. 'Good. I have been waiting a long time for this fight. Not with you — with him.' He points behind you, as if there stands the Great Sage Equal to Heaven who once called him brother. The bonds between the Bull Demon King and Sun Wukong go back five hundred years, to the sworn brotherhood of the demon realm. Seven great demons became brothers — the Bull Demon King, the Sea-Covering Great Sage, the Sky-Confounding Great Sage, the Mountain-Moving Great Sage, the Wind-Penetrating Great Sage, the God-Expelling Great Sage, and the Great Sage Equal to Heaven. What glorious names those seven were — but now they have gone, scattered, or died. Only he and that golden staff remain. This battle is fought over brotherhood. The Bull Demon King's raw strength exceeds all imagination. Each stomp splits the earth; each punch sends a gale-force wind. Before him, you are but a moth. But you have more than a moth — you have the Fiery Golden Eyes, the Wind-Following Ears, a tongue that has tasted every flavor, and a heart of iron. You see the tremor in his muscles before each punch, hear the rhythm of his breath before each attack, your body instinctively dodging. Finally, you leap onto his arm, run up that limb thicker than a tree trunk, and deliver a crushing blow to the back of his neck — The Bull Demon King drops to one knee, splitting the earth three spans. He does not fall, but kneels there, panting heavily. After a long while, he pulls a golden orb from his bosom and hands it to you — the Body Root. 'Take it. What he owed me, you do not need to repay.' Then he rises slowly and walks into the depths of Flaming Mountain without looking back. Clutching that orb, you feel a weight of power for the first time. The Body Root makes you stronger, tougher — but not just physically. Your heart as well. You begin to understand why the Great Sage gave up his Buddha seat and returned to the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit — not out of pride, not out of rebellion, but out of weariness with being 'arranged.' He, too, wanted to be a free monkey. And as you lift your gaze — amid the receding flames stand several不朽 buildings. Shuozhou's Buddha Palace Temple Sakyamuni Pagoda has stood here for nearly a thousand years. This world's tallest pure-wooden pavilion-style pagoda, sixty-seven meters high without a single iron nail, relying entirely on interlocking bracket sets and tenon-mortise joints, standing tall through earthquakes and wars — it teaches you this kind of unyielding resilience. A furnace brick fell and became the Flaming Mountain, the red lotus's karmic fire illuminates each pass.
The Bull Demon kneels and mountains and rivers shake — with the Body Root in hand, true toil begins at last.

stops.title: Final Chapter: Western Paradise · Thunderclap Monastery — Destiny Restored
stops.content: You have traveled very, very far. Over Flaming Mountain, through Flowing Sands River, across countless mountain passes. Five roots in hand, only one remains — the Mind Root. You finally reach Western Cattle-Horn Continent. The Thunderclap Monastery lies ahead. But this Monastery is not as you imagined — it is empty. Tathagata has left, all the Buddhas have left, leaving only a magnificent yet desolate mountain gate. The entire monastery is built into the mountain, rising layer upon layer, every brick and stone steeped in the passage of time. As you stand at the foot looking up, the shock is indescribable — because the architecture of this 'Black Myth Thunderclap Monastery' draws from two real places. Shanxi Ruicheng's Yongle Palace, world-famous for its Yuan-dynasty murals — the 'Court Pilgrimage' in the Sanqing Hall features over eight hundred deities marching in procession, their robes billowing, their lines flowing endlessly — that grand composition is the inspiration for the Thunderclap Monastery's empty, majestic feel. Tianjin Jizhou's Dule Temple, where the Liao-dynasty Guanyin Pavilion towers into the clouds, the eleven-faced Guanyin statue dropping from the top of the pavilion all the way to the bottom — that sense of 'looking up at a giant Buddha' is precisely what you feel standing before the Thunderclap Monastery's mountain gate: small and insignificant before the vast Buddha architecture, the mix of oppression and sacredness leaves you breathless. Entering the gate, you climb the stone steps. On the cliffs on either side, you see traces of layered carvings — Buddha figures, bodhisattvas, Dharma-protecting deva kings, all worn soft by a thousand years of weathering. This textural effect comes from two thousand-year-old grottoes in Chongqing's Dazu — Beishan Cliff Carvings and Baodingshan Cliff Carvings. Dazu's grottoes are the pinnacle of late Chinese cave art: Beishan saw nearly three centuries of uninterrupted carving from late Tang to Southern Song, nearly ten thousand statues densely embedded in a crescent-shaped cliff face, each one an aesthetic archive of its era; Baodingshan was designed by Southern Song monk Zhao Zhifeng as a complete cliff-side narrative system, from the 'Six Realms of Rebirth' to 'Modes of Hell' — each group of carvings tells a story like a comic strip. Dazu's artisans turned the entire mountain into a stone-carved Buddhist encyclopedia. These expressions worn by time are the perfect prototypes for the fragmentary Buddhas on the walls of the Black Myth Thunderclap Monastery. Continuing upward, past layered platforms, you reach an open area halfway up the mountain, dotted with complete halls — Pingyao's outlying Zhenguo Temple's Ten-Thousand-Buddha Hall, a Five-Dynasties wooden structure still intact, one of the few remaining Five-Dynasties examples in China, which Liang Sicheng called 'uniquely ancient in form, truly rare.' Deep in Wutai Mountain, Wutai Mountain Nanshan Temple rises seven stories, every wall covered in exquisite stone carvings, from Buddhist stories to flowers, birds, fish, and insects — a treasure-house of Wutai Mountain stone carving. Pingyao's Shuanglin Temple needs no introduction — over two thousand Song and Yuan colored sculptures fill ten halls, the Thousand-Buddha Hall's Skanda statue curved like a bow, his robes seeming to fly — that statue, praised as 'the finest Skanda in the nation,' is just a pile of clay, yet more alive than any living person. Even placed as a boss in Black Myth, it would not be out of place. In the dim light of the Thunderclap Monastery, these stone carvings and colored sculptures seem to come alive. Every Buddha statue watches you. Every bodhisattva waits for you to answer that question. You finally reach the summit. The Mahavira Hall of the Thunderclap Monastery stands before you. The doors are wide open, revealing total darkness within. You take a deep breath, grip your golden staff tightly, and step inside. From the depths of the hall, a figure slowly emerges from the darkness. Not Tathagata, not the Jade Emperor — it is yourself. Or rather, the Great Sage you have been seeking all along. He sits on the Buddha seat, not rising. He simply looks at you and smiles. 'You have come. I have waited long for you. 'Do you think I scattered my Six Roots so you could gather them and revive me? Wrong. I did it so that you could — become me. Every step you have taken, every battle you have fought, every Buddha you have seen — all were asking yourself: Who are you? 'Now, you must answer. Who are you?' You say nothing. You simply walk forward, approach the Buddha seat, reach out, and gently grasp the golden staff resting on his knee. The moment your fingers touch the staff, the entire Thunderclap Monastery begins to tremble. Golden light bursts from all directions. Every fragmentary Buddha on the stone walls opens its eyes. Every tile and brick begins to glow. Beijing Shijingshan's
stops.poem:
Yongle's paintings built the Thunderclap hall, Dazu's stone carvings carve into the soul.
Six Roots united, the Mind Root made whole — destiny lies in the self, beyond all control.
